claim: Human perivascular stem cells (PSCs) were purified from adipose tissue by FACS selection of CD34+CD146-CD45-CD31- adventitial progenitor cells and CD146+CD34-CD45-CD31- pericytes.
source: Perivascular stem/stromal cells (PSCs) were derived from human white adipose tissue using previously reported methods, by FACS selection of the related populations of CD34+CD146-CD45-CD31- adventitial progenitor cells and CD146+CD34-CD45-CD31- pericytes (Corselli et al., 2012; Crisan et al., 2008; James et al., 2017a; Meyers et al., 2018aMeyers et al., 2018b; Meyers et al., 2018b) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the methodology described in the text and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1, which shows the FACS gating strategy. The method is also supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: PSCs induced significant mitogenic effects on BMSCs when placed in non-contact co-culture conditions.
source: Co-culture results showed that PSCs induced significant mitogenic (Figure 1A, MTS assay), pro-migratory (Figure 1B, scratch wound healing assay), and pro-osteogenic effects (Figure 1C, alkaline phosphatase activity) on BMSCs when placed in non-contact co-culture conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A using MTS assay to measure cell proliferation in transwell co-culture experiments.

claim: PSCs induced significant pro-migratory effects on BMSCs when placed in non-contact co-culture conditions.
source: Co-culture results showed that PSCs induced significant mitogenic (Figure 1A, MTS assay), pro-migratory (Figure 1B, scratch wound healing assay), and pro-osteogenic effects (Figure 1C, alkaline phosphatase activity) on BMSCs when placed in non-contact co-culture conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B using scratch wound healing assay to measure cell migration in transwell co-culture experiments.

claim: PSCs induced significant pro-osteogenic effects on BMSCs when placed in non-contact co-culture conditions.
source: Co-culture results showed that PSCs induced significant mitogenic (Figure 1A, MTS assay), pro-migratory (Figure 1B, scratch wound healing assay), and pro-osteogenic effects (Figure 1C, alkaline phosphatase activity) on BMSCs when placed in non-contact co-culture conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C using alkaline phosphatase activity assay to measure osteogenic differentiation in transwell co-culture experiments.

claim: PKH26 lipophilic dye from PSCs was incorporated into BMSCs under non-contact culture conditions, suggesting exchange of membrane from parent PSCs to recipient cells.
source: When a lipophilic dye (PKH26) was used to label the cell membrane of PSCs, this dye was incorporated into the BMSCs, suggesting the exchange of membrane from parent PSCs to recipient cells under non-contact culture conditions (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1D demonstrating transfer of PKH26 dye from labeled PSCs to unlabeled BMSCs in transwell co-culture.

claim: PSC-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs) have spherical morphology as observed by transmission electron microscopy.
source: Spherical PSC-EV morphology was observed by transmission EM (Figure 1E), with enrichment of tetraspanin molecule expression (CD9, CD63, and CD81), but without expression of the endoplasmic reticulum protein calnexin (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by transmission electron microscopy images shown in Figure 1E.

claim: PSC-EVs are enriched in tetraspanin molecules CD9, CD63, and CD81.
source: Spherical PSC-EV morphology was observed by transmission EM (Figure 1E), with enrichment of tetraspanin molecule expression (CD9, CD63, and CD81), but without expression of the endoplasmic reticulum protein calnexin (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1F demonstrating expression of CD9, CD63, and CD81 in PSC-EVs.

claim: PSC-EVs do not express the endoplasmic reticulum protein calnexin.
source: Spherical PSC-EV morphology was observed by transmission EM (Figure 1E), with enrichment of tetraspanin molecule expression (CD9, CD63, and CD81), but without expression of the endoplasmic reticulum protein calnexin (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1F demonstrating absence of calnexin expression in PSC-EVs while present in cell lysate.

claim: The size distribution of PSC-EVs is most commonly approximately 100 nm.
source: Size distribution of PSC-EVs was most commonly ~100 nm, as shown by either TEM quantification (Figure 1G) or nanoparticle tracking analysis (NanoSight) (Figure 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by size distribution data from both TEM quantification (Figure 1G) and nanoparticle tracking analysis (Figure 1H).

claim: EV yield per PSC per day as assessed by protein content was 1.11 ± 0.18 pg.
source: EV yield per cell per day as assessed by protein content was 1.11 ± 0.18 pg, as determined by the Bradford method (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by protein quantification data using the Bradford method.

claim: 10,256 annotated genes were expressed in all samples of PSC-EVs and parent PSCs among 54,136 total RNA transcripts.
source: Among these, 10,256 annotated genes were expressed in all samples of 54,136 total RNA transcripts (19% of total, including 10,256 protein coding RNA; six non-coding RNA; and four pseudo RNA).
evidence: The claim is supported by total RNA sequencing data comparing PSC-EVs to parent PSCs.

claim: Clear separation between gene expression profiles was observed when comparing PSC-EV RNA content to their parent cells.
source: Clear separation between gene expression profiles were observed when comparing PSC-EV RNA content to their parent cells, as observed by unsupervised hierarchical clustering (Figure 1I) and principal component analysis (Figure 1J).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA sequencing data analyzed by unsupervised hierarchical clustering (Figure 1I) and principal component analysis (Figure 1J).

claim: Higher expression of most putative perivascular MSC marker transcripts was seen in PSCs compared to PSC-EVs.
source: Putative gene markers of human perivascular MSC were cross-referenced within PSCs and PSC-EVs (Cho et al., 2017). Higher expression of most transcripts were seen in each PSC isolate (such as CD44, NT5E, ENG, LEPR, PDGFRA, and PDGFRB), with comparatively less expression among PSC-EVs (Figure 1K).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1K comparing expression of perivascular markers between PSCs and PSC-EVs, with reference to prior literature (Cho et al., 2017).

claim: The highest expressing 100 genes within PSC-EVs were all protein coding genes.
source: The highest expressing 100 genes within PSC-EVs are listed in Supplementary file 4. All 100 were protein coding genes, 57 encoded for ribosomal proteins (e.g. RPS18, RPL37A, and RPL41) and 68 were included within Gene Ontology term extracellular exosome (GO term: 0070062).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA sequencing data analysis identifying the top 100 expressed genes in PSC-EVs.

claim: 57 of the highest expressing 100 genes within PSC-EVs encoded for ribosomal proteins.
source: The highest expressing 100 genes within PSC-EVs are listed in Supplementary file 4. All 100 were protein coding genes, 57 encoded for ribosomal proteins (e.g. RPS18, RPL37A, and RPL41) and 68 were included within Gene Ontology term extracellular exosome (GO term: 0070062).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA sequencing data analysis and Gene Ontology annotation of the top 100 expressed genes in PSC-EVs.

claim: 68 of the highest expressing 100 genes within PSC-EVs were included within Gene Ontology term extracellular exosome.
source: The highest expressing 100 genes within PSC-EVs are listed in Supplementary file 4. All 100 were protein coding genes, 57 encoded for ribosomal proteins (e.g. RPS18, RPL37A, and RPL41) and 68 were included within Gene Ontology term extracellular exosome (GO term: 0070062).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA sequencing data analysis and Gene Ontology annotation of the top 100 expressed genes in PSC-EVs.

claim: Highly expressed PSC-EV transcripts included several genes associated with adipocytes or adipogenesis.
source: Reflecting their adipose tissue origin, these highly expressed PSC-EV transcripts included several genes associated with adipocytes or adipogenesis, such as VIM, RACK1, and LGALS1.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA sequencing data analysis identifying highly expressed genes in PSC-EVs and their known biological functions.

claim: Highly expressed PSC-EV genes included transcripts involved in the regulation of cellular proliferation.
source: Highly expressed PSC-EV genes also included transcripts involved in the regulation of cellular proliferation (e.g. FTL, RAB13, MT2A, and TMSB10) or cellular migration (e.g. RAB13, TMSB10, S100A6, and EEF1A1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA sequencing data analysis identifying highly expressed genes in PSC-EVs and their known biological functions.

claim: Highly expressed PSC-EV genes included transcripts involved in cellular migration.
source: Highly expressed PSC-EV genes also included transcripts involved in the regulation of cellular proliferation (e.g. FTL, RAB13, MT2A, and TMSB10) or cellular migration (e.g. RAB13, TMSB10, S100A6, and EEF1A1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA sequencing data analysis identifying highly expressed genes in PSC-EVs and their known biological functions.

claim: Of 39 transcription factors enriched in porcine adipose tissue stem/stromal cell (ASC)-EVs, 14 genes (35.9%) were also enriched in human PSC-EVs.
source: Next, PSC-EV RNA content was cross-referenced to a previously published RNA Seq dataset within unpurified adipose stromal cell-derived EVs from porcine tissue (Eirin et al., 2014). As expected, some overlap existed in EV content between these two adipose stromal cell derivatives (Supplementary file 5). For example, of 39 transcription factors previously found to be enriched in adipose tissue stem/stromal cell (ASC)-EVs (Eirin et al., 2014), 14 genes (35.9%) were also enriched in human PSC-EVs.
evidence: The claim is supported by cross-referencing RNA sequencing data from human PSC-EVs with previously published data from porcine ASC-EVs (Eirin et al., 2014).

claim: Known positive regulators of cellular proliferation were identified among transcription factors enriched in both porcine ASC-EVs and human PSC-EVs.
source: Of these, known positive regulators of cellular proliferation (e.g. JMJD1C, NRIP1, and TRPS1) and cellular migration (e.g. JMJD1C, TCF4, and KLF7) were identified.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA sequencing data analysis and known biological functions of identified transcription factors.

claim: Known positive regulators of cellular migration were identified among transcription factors enriched in both porcine ASC-EVs and human PSC-EVs.
source: Of these, known positive regulators of cellular proliferation (e.g. JMJD1C, NRIP1, and TRPS1) and cellular migration (e.g. JMJD1C, TCF4, and KLF7) were identified.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA sequencing data analysis and known biological functions of identified transcription factors.

claim: Several transcriptional repressors found within previously published ASC-EVs were not found at high levels in human PSC-EVs.
source: Of note, several transcriptional repressors were found within the previously published ASC-EVs (e.g. ZNF568, ZHX1, ZBTB1, and RUNX1T1), which were not found at high levels in human PSC-EVs.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative RNA sequencing data analysis between human PSC-EVs and previously published porcine ASC-EVs.

claim: PKH26-labeled PSC-EVs were internalized by human BMSCs after 48 hr, as shown by cytosolic fluorescence distribution.
source: To demonstrate interaction of EVs with the recipient cells, PSC-EVs were first labeled with PKH26 dye, and fluorescently labeled PSC-EVs were directly applied to human BMSCs. After 48 hr, fluorescence was observed on the recipient BMSCs in a cytosolic distribution (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2A demonstrating PKH26 fluorescence in BMSCs after PSC-EV treatment.

claim: pHrodo Red Maleimide-labeled PSC-EVs were internalized by recipient BMSCs after 48 hr, as shown by fluorescence in an acidic environment.
source: PSC-EVs were next labeled with a pH dependent dye (pHrodo Red Maleimide), which only fluoresces after exposure to an acidic environment such as the cellular interior (Figure 2B). After 48 hr, fluorescence was again observed suggesting EV internalization by the recipient BMSCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2B demonstrating pHrodo fluorescence in BMSCs after PSC-EV treatment, indicating internalization into acidic compartments.

claim: PSC-EVs exerted a dose-dependent mitogenic effect on recipient BMSCs.
source: PSC-EVs exerted a dose-dependent mitogenic effect on recipient BMSCs (Figures 2C and 1, 2.5, and 5 μg/mL, MTS assays).
evidence: The claim is supported by MTS assay data shown in Figure 2C demonstrating increased cell proliferation with increasing PSC-EV concentrations.

claim: PSC-EVs represented a significant pro-migratory stimulus for BMSCs, with the lowest PSC-EV concentration demonstrating the largest effect.
source: Using a scratch wound healing assay, PSC-EVs represented a significant pro-migratory stimulus, with the lowest PSC-EV concentration demonstrating the largest effect (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by scratch wound healing assay data shown in Figure 2D demonstrating increased cell migration with PSC-EV treatment, with maximal effect at the lowest concentration.

claim: PSC-EVs induced a dose dependent increase in ALP activity under osteogenic differentiation conditions.
source: Under osteogenic differentiation conditions, PSC-EVs induced a dose dependent increase in ALP activity (Figure 2E) and bone nodule deposition (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by alkaline phosphatase activity assay data shown in Figure 2E demonstrating increased ALP activity with increasing PSC-EV concentrations.

claim: PSC-EVs induced a dose dependent increase in bone nodule deposition under osteogenic differentiation conditions.
source: Under osteogenic differentiation conditions, PSC-EVs induced a dose dependent increase in ALP activity (Figure 2E) and bone nodule deposition (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by Alizarin Red staining data shown in Figure 2F demonstrating increased mineralization with increasing PSC-EV concentrations.

claim: PSC-EVs induced a dose-dependent positive regulatory effect on osteoblastic gene markers RUNX2 and SP7.
source: Quantitative PCR analysis of characteristic osteoblastic gene markers confirmed a dose-dependent positive regulatory effect by PSC-EVs (Figure 2G), including RUNX2 (Runt related transcription factor 2) and SP7 (Osterix).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2G demonstrating increased expression of RUNX2 and SP7 with increasing PSC-EV concentrations.

claim: The mitogenic effect of PSC-EVs was not observed among recipient ASCs, unlike BMSCs.
source: We next queried as to whether recipient stromal cells responded to PSC-EVs in a tissue-specific manner. Here, human culture-derived ASCs were exposed to the identical PSC-EV treatment conditions with broad similarities and minor differences found (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). Unlike BMSCs, the mitogenic effect of PSC-EVs was not observed among recipient ASCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative MTS assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 demonstrating differential proliferative responses between BMSCs and ASCs to PSC-EV treatment.

claim: The pro-migratory and pro-osteogenic effects of PSC-EVs were conserved findings across both BMSC and ASC recipient stromal cells.
source: The pro-migratory and pro-osteogenic effects of PSC-EVs were conserved findings across both recipient stromal cells, although the maximum efficacious dose for each bioactivity assay was different when comparing BM- and AT-derived recipient cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative functional assay data across BMSCs and ASCs shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: ASC-EVs exerted mitogenic, pro-migratory, and pro-osteogenic effects on recipient BMSCs.
source: Finally, we compared the effects of EVs from unsorted ASCs and homogeneous PSCs on recipient BMSCs. Like PSC-EVs, ASC-EVs exerted mitogenic, pro-migratory, and pro-osteogenic effects on recipient BMSCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by functional assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 comparing ASC-EVs and PSC-EVs effects on BMSCs.

claim: The magnitude of bioactive effects was significantly different between ASC-EV and PSC-EV preparations on recipient BMSCs.
source: However, the magnitude of change was significantly different between EV preparations, and PSC-EVs demonstrated a stronger induction of cell proliferation and osteogenic differentiation, while ASC-EVs enhanced cell migration to a greater degree.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative functional assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 demonstrating quantitative differences in bioactivity between ASC-EVs and PSC-EVs.

claim: 38,416 annotated genes were expressed in all samples among 135,750 total probesets in the BMSC transcriptome analysis.
source: 38,416 annotated genes were expressed in all samples among 135,750 total probesets (20,014 protein coding RNA; 5054 non-coding RNA; 2795 pseudo RNA; 207 sno RNA; 55 snRNA; 26 rRNA; two scRNA).
evidence: The claim is supported by Affymetrix Clariom D microarray data analyzing the BMSC transcriptome after PSC-EV treatment.

claim: Clear differences between control- and PSC-EV-treated BMSC gene expression were observed by unsupervised hierarchical clustering and principal component analysis.
source: Clear differences between control- and PSC-EV-treated BMSC gene expression were observed by unsupervised hierarchical clustering (Figure 2H) and principal component analysis (Figure 2I).
evidence: The claim is supported by microarray data analysis shown in Figure 2H and 2I demonstrating distinct gene expression profiles between control and PSC-EV-treated BMSCs.

claim: 4129 transcripts showed >2 SD increase in expression with PSC-EV treatment (3.04% of total).
source: As shown by volcano plot (Figure 2J), 4129 transcripts showed >2 SD increase in expression with PSC-EV treatment (3.04% of total, red dots), while 2589 transcripts showed >2 SD reduction in expression with PSC-EV treatment (1.91% of total, blue dots).
evidence: The claim is supported by microarray data analysis shown in Figure 2J volcano plot.

claim: 2589 transcripts showed >2 SD reduction in expression with PSC-EV treatment (1.91% of total).
source: As shown by volcano plot (Figure 2J), 4129 transcripts showed >2 SD increase in expression with PSC-EV treatment (3.04% of total, red dots), while 2589 transcripts showed >2 SD reduction in expression with PSC-EV treatment (1.91% of total, blue dots).
evidence: The claim is supported by microarray data analysis shown in Figure 2J volcano plot.

claim: The majority of activated pathways in PSC-EV-treated BMSCs were associated with positive regulation of cell proliferation, migration, and/or osteogenesis.
source: QIAGEN Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA) showed that the majority of the activated pathways were associated with the positive regulation of cell proliferation, migration, and/or osteogenesis, including for example SAPK/JNK signaling (Zha et al., 2016), HGF signaling (Forte et al., 2006), Sirtuin signaling (Simic et al., 2013), FGF Signaling (Gharibi and Hughes, 2012), and PDGF Signaling (Li et al., 2014), among recipient BMSCs (Figure 2K, see Supplementary file 6 for a complete list).
evidence: The claim is supported by Ingenuity Pathway Analysis of microarray data shown in Figure 2K, with supporting citations for the biological functions of identified pathways.

claim: Downregulated signaling pathways among recipient BMSCs included those known to negatively regulate cell proliferation, such as AMPK Signaling and PTEN signaling.
source: Conversely, downregulated signaling pathways among recipient BMSCs included those known to negatively regulate cell proliferation, such as AMPK Signaling (de Meester et al., 2014). PTEN signaling was also downregulated, which negatively regulates BMSC proliferation (Shen et al., 2018), migration (Comer and Parent, 2002) and osteogenic differentiation (Liu et al., 2017) (Figure 2K, see Supplementary file 7 for a complete list).
evidence: The claim is supported by Ingenuity Pathway Analysis of microarray data shown in Figure 2K, with supporting citations for the biological functions of identified pathways.

claim: Of 7789 PSC-EV transcripts with a mean FPKM >0, approximately half (3678 transcripts, 47.22%) were increased among PSC-EV-treated BMSCs.
source: Next, the transcriptome of PSC-EVs (as previously determined by RNA-Seq) was cross-referenced to changes within the BMSC transcriptome after EV treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 3). Here, of 7789 PSC-EV transcripts with a mean FPKM >0, approximately half of these transcripts demonstrated were increased among PSC-EV-treated BMSCs (3678 transcripts, 47.22% of total).
evidence: The claim is supported by cross-referencing RNA-Seq data from PSC-EVs with microarray data from PSC-EV-treated BMSCs, as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Global changes in the recipient BMSC transcriptome were not well explained by simple transfer of EV RNA cargo.
source: Thus, global changes in the recipient BMSC transcriptome were not well explained by simple transfer of EV RNA cargo.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that only about half of PSC-EV transcripts were increased in treated BMSCs, suggesting more complex regulatory mechanisms.

claim: Pretreatment with trypsin completely abrogated the mitogenic effects of PSC-EVs.
source: Pretreatment with trypsin completely abrogated the mitogenic (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), pro-migratory (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), and pro-osteogenic effects of PSC-EVs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by MTS assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A comparing untreated and trypsinized PSC-EVs.

claim: Pretreatment with trypsin completely abrogated the pro-migratory effects of PSC-EVs.
source: Pretreatment with trypsin completely abrogated the mitogenic (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), pro-migratory (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), and pro-osteogenic effects of PSC-EVs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by scratch wound healing assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B comparing untreated and trypsinized PSC-EVs.

claim: Pretreatment with trypsin completely abrogated the pro-osteogenic effects of PSC-EVs.
source: Pretreatment with trypsin completely abrogated the mitogenic (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), pro-migratory (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), and pro-osteogenic effects of PSC-EVs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Alizarin Red staining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C comparing untreated and trypsinized PSC-EVs.

claim: Surface-associated vesicular proteins are integral for PSC-EV bioactivity.
source: Thus, surface-associated vesicular proteins are integral for PSC-EV bioactivity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that trypsin treatment, which digests surface proteins, completely abrogated all bioactive effects of PSC-EVs.

claim: Anti-CD9 and anti-CD81 neutralizing antibodies prevented EV internalization by recipient BMSCs.
source: PSC-EVs were labeled with a pH dependent dye and treated with or without neutralizing antibodies (Figure 3). After 48 hr and in contrast to control conditions, minimal fluorescence was seen with either neutralizing antibody, suggesting that CD9 and CD81 were required for EV internalization (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3A demonstrating reduced pHrodo fluorescence in BMSCs when PSC-EVs were pre-treated with anti-CD9 or anti-CD81 antibodies.

claim: Both anti-CD9 and anti-CD81 neutralizing antibodies reversed the mitogenic effects of PSC-EVs.
source: Results demonstrated that both anti-CD9 and anti-CD81 reversed the mitogenic effects of PSC-EVs (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by MTS assay data shown in Figure 3B and 3C demonstrating loss of proliferative effects when PSC-EVs were pre-treated with neutralizing antibodies.

claim: The pro-migratory effects of PSC-EVs were completely abrogated by either anti-CD9 or anti-CD81 neutralizing antibodies.
source: Likewise, the pro-migratory effects of PSC-EVs were completely abrogated by either neutralizing antibody (Figure 3D–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by scratch wound healing assay data shown in Figure 3D-G demonstrating loss of migratory effects when PSC-EVs were pre-treated with neutralizing antibodies.

claim: The pro-osteogenic effects of PSC-EVs were partially reversed by anti-CD9 neutralizing antibodies.
source: The pro-osteogenic effects of PSC-EVs were partially reversed by anti-CD9 (Figure 3H,I), but not anti-CD81 neutralizing antibodies (Figure 3J,K).
evidence: The claim is supported by Alizarin Red staining data shown in Figure 3H and 3I demonstrating partial reduction of osteogenic effects when PSC-EVs were pre-treated with anti-CD9 antibodies.

claim: The pro-osteogenic effects of PSC-EVs were not reversed by anti-CD81 neutralizing antibodies.
source: The pro-osteogenic effects of PSC-EVs were partially reversed by anti-CD9 (Figure 3H,I), but not anti-CD81 neutralizing antibodies (Figure 3J,K).
evidence: The claim is supported by Alizarin Red staining data shown in Figure 3J and 3K demonstrating no significant reduction of osteogenic effects when PSC-EVs were pre-treated with anti-CD81 antibodies.

claim: Intact activity of CD9 or CD81 are essential for the majority of bioactive effects of PSC-EVs on recipient osteoprogenitor cells.
source: In sum, intact activity of CD9 or CD81 are essential for the majority of bioactive effects of PSC-EVs on recipient osteoprogenitor cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the collective data showing that neutralizing antibodies against CD9 or CD81 abrogated most bioactive effects of PSC-EVs.

claim: shRNA-mediated knockdown achieved 52.9% reduction of IGSF8 gene expression in human BMSCs.
source: In a candidate fashion, shRNA-mediated knockdown of IGSF8 and PTGFRN was performed in human recipient BMSCs (Figure 4A, 52.9% and 58.4% knockdown of IGSF8 and PTGFRN gene expression, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by PCR data shown in Figure 4A demonstrating reduced IGSF8 expression after shRNA treatment.

claim: shRNA-mediated knockdown achieved 58.4% reduction of PTGFRN gene expression in human BMSCs.
source: In a candidate fashion, shRNA-mediated knockdown of IGSF8 and PTGFRN was performed in human recipient BMSCs (Figure 4A, 52.9% and 58.4% knockdown of IGSF8 and PTGFRN gene expression, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by PCR data shown in Figure 4A demonstrating reduced PTGFRN expression after shRNA treatment.

claim: No fluorescence was seen among BMSCs with IGSF8 or PTGFRN knockdown after 48 hr incubation with pH-dependent dye-labeled PSC-EVs.
source: PSC-EVs were labeled with a pH-dependent dye and incubated with BMSCs with or without knockdown. After 48 hr and unlike vector control conditions, no fluorescence was seen among BMSCs with IGSF8 or PTGFRN knockdown (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4B demonstrating absence of pHrodo fluorescence in BMSCs with IGSF8 or PTGFRN knockdown.

claim: Knockdown of either IGSF8 or PTGFRN abrogated the mitogenic effects of PSC-EVs.
source: In comparison to vector control, knockdown of either IGSF8 or PTGFRN abrogated the mitogenic effects of PSC-EVs (Figure 4C, 2.5 μg/mL PSC-EVs used).
evidence: The claim is supported by MTS assay data shown in Figure 4C demonstrating loss of proliferative effects of PSC-EVs in BMSCs with IGSF8 or PTGFRN knockdown.

claim: IGSF8 or PTGFRN knockdown nullified the pro-migratory effect of PSC-EVs.
source: Likewise, IGSF8 or PTGFRN KD nullified the pro-migratory effect of PSC-EVs (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by scratch wound healing assay data shown in Figure 4D demonstrating loss of migratory effects of PSC-EVs in BMSCs with IGSF8 or PTGFRN knockdown.

claim: PTGFRN knockdown inhibited the pro-osteogenic effect of PSC-EVs.
source: Finally, PTGFRN KD inhibited the pro-osteogenic effect of PSC-EVs (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Alizarin Red staining data shown in Figure 4E demonstrating loss of osteogenic effects of PSC-EVs in BMSCs with PTGFRN knockdown.

claim: IGSF8 knockdown paradoxically increased BMSC osteogenic differentiation in both control and PSC-EV treatment conditions.
source: In contrast, IGSF8 KD paradoxically increased BMSC osteogenic differentiation; however, this was observed in both control and PSC-EV treatment conditions and therefore appeared to be an EV independent phenomenon.
evidence: The claim is supported by Alizarin Red staining data shown in Figure 4E demonstrating increased osteogenic differentiation with IGSF8 knockdown regardless of PSC-EV treatment.

claim: EV-associated CD9 and CD81 along with their known binding partners on the recipient cell are required for the majority of bioactive effects of perivascular EVs.
source: Thus and in aggregate, EV-associated CD9 and CD81 along with their known binding partners on the recipient cell are required for the majority of bioactive effects of perivascular EVs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the collective data showing that neutralizing antibodies against CD9/CD81 and knockdown of their binding partners IGSF8/PTGFRN abrogated most bioactive effects of PSC-EVs.

claim: PSC-EVs treatment resulted in mitogenic, pro-migratory, and pro-osteogenic effects on mouse ASCs.
source: In similarity to human recipient cells, PSC-EVs treatment resulted in similar mitogenic, pro-migratory, and pro-osteogenic effects on both mouse ASCs and NMCCs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by functional assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 demonstrating bioactive effects of PSC-EVs on mouse ASCs.

claim: PSC-EVs treatment resulted in mitogenic, pro-migratory, and pro-osteogenic effects on neonatal mouse calvarial cells (NMCCs).
source: In similarity to human recipient cells, PSC-EVs treatment resulted in similar mitogenic, pro-migratory, and pro-osteogenic effects on both mouse ASCs and NMCCs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by functional assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 demonstrating bioactive effects of PSC-EVs on NMCCs.

claim: PSC-EV-treated defects showed an increase in osteoblastic proliferation at the bone defect edge, as shown by Ki67 immunostaining.
source: PSC-EV-treated defects showed an increase in osteoblastic proliferation at the bone defect edge, as shown by Ki67 immunostaining and quantitation of immunoreactive cells at the bone defect edge (Figure 5A,B, appearing red with arrowheads).
evidence: The claim is supported by Ki67 immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A and quantification in Figure 5B demonstrating increased proliferation at the defect edge with PSC-EV treatment.

claim: PSC-EV-treated defects showed a prominent increase in GFP+ stromal progenitor cell migration into the defect mid-substance in Pdgfrα-CreER;eGFP animals.
source: In order to assess progenitor cell migration into the defect, a lineage tracing strategy was employed using Pdgfrα-CreER;eGFP animals (Figure 5C). Reporter activity within Pdgfrα-CreER;eGFP highlights bone-lining stromal cells which then migrate into populate the bone injury site. PSC-EV-treated defects showed a prominent increase in GFP+ stromal progenitor cell migration into the defect mid-substance (Figure 5C,D, quantified right as the mean fluorescence intensity within the middle of the defect site).
evidence: The claim is supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 5C and quantification in Figure 5D demonstrating increased GFP+ cell migration with PSC-EV treatment.

claim: Microcomputed tomography (μCT) reconstructions revealed an increase in defect re-ossification with PSC-EV treatment in comparison to PBS control.
source: Microcomputed tomography (μCT) reconstructions revealed an increase in defect re-ossification in comparison to PBS control (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by μCT imaging data shown in Figure 5E demonstrating increased bone formation with PSC-EV treatment.

claim: Quantitative μCT indices confirmed an increase in bone healing across all metrics, including bone volume (BV), bone formation area (BFA), and semi-quantitative healing score.
source: Quantitative indices confirmed an increase in bone healing across all metrics, including bone volume (BV, Figure 5F), bone formation area (BFA, Figure 5G), and semi-quantitative healing score (Figure 5H) (Spicer et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative μCT analysis data shown in Figure 5F-H demonstrating increased bone healing metrics with PSC-EV treatment, with reference to the healing score methodology (Spicer et al., 2012).

claim: H&E staining confirmed a significant narrowing of the gap between bony fronts with PSC-EV treatment.
